--- engine: knitr filters: - webr webr: show-startup-message: true cell-options: autorun: true --- # Project Closeout and Termination ## Learning Objectives By the end of this chapter you will be able to: 1. **State** what project termination provides and distinguish its types --- extinction, addition, integration, starvation. 2. **Work through** the seven elements of closeout. 3. **Explain** what commonly prevents effective closeout. 4. **Recognize** the early warning signs of project failure. 5. **Apply** the cancel/continue decision using sunk cost, cost-to-complete, and remaining benefit. 6. **Reconcile** a completed project: planned vs. actual schedule and cost. 7. **Draw** the common lessons from famous project failures.
Before we begin: which is harder --- starting a project or finishing one? Starting has energy and a blank page. Finishing has a tired team, a client eager to move on, and a next project already calling. Closeout is *"the most difficult phase to complete effectively and has the most impact on future projects."*
## Introduction: planning for extinction A defining feature of a project is a **finite life**. When you plan a project, you are also *"planning for its extinction."* The RC-vehicle prototype project will end --- and if it succeeds, its team likely rolls straight into supporting the 100 000-unit production run. That is a real, named way for a project to end, not an afterthought. **Project termination** provides for: - **Acceptance** of the project by the sponsor - **Completion** of the project records - **Final revision and issue** of documentation to its as-built condition - **Retention** of the essential documentation --- above all, the **lessons learned**
## Types of termination ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning: The `label.size` argument of `geom_label()` is deprecated as of ggplot2 3.5.0. ℹ Please use the `linewidth` argument instead. ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Four ways a project ends. Extinction, addition, and integration are normal; starvation is a slow, deliberate neglect.](13-Project-Closeout-and-Termination_files/figure-html/fig-termination-types-13-1.png){#fig-termination-types-13 fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: - **Extinction** --- the project is stopped, successfully or not. The final budget is audited, team members get new assignments, material assets are dispersed or transferred per company/contract terms. - **Addition** --- a successful project is made a **formal part of the organization**. An automaker that has launched a new vehicle keeps the project team on as a **production support team**. - **Integration** --- the team and resources are **reabsorbed** into the existing structure. Common but complicated --- and organizations often **lose key people** here, who leave for fresh project challenges rather than return to the old department. - **Starvation** --- not really a termination act but *"a willful form of neglect"*: the budget is decreased slowly until the project cannot remain viable. Kept "on the books" for political reasons, a powerful sponsor's pet project, or so it can be reactivated when budgets recover. ### Try it yourself: which way did the project end? ```{=html}
``` ## The seven elements of closeout ::: {#tbl-closeout-13 .cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
The seven elements of project closeout.
# Element What
1 Verify scope Compare to the original scope statement; resolve discrepancies; confirm every deliverable is present; assess customer satisfaction.
2 Closeout contracts Resolve all open issues with the customer; return or destroy proprietary documents as directed; receive final payments. The client is a future customer -- leave them feeling good.
3 Closeout administration Return all loaned personnel; complete performance evaluations.
4 Conduct a lessons-learned review Survey everyone who was on the project; hold the meeting; be critical -- dissect what went wrong and why, not what went right.
5 Build a project history file Document planned vs. actual schedule and cost (with reasons), approved changes, meeting minutes, WBS, risk plans, subcontractor and customer-satisfaction records, reviews.
6 Create the final project report Document overall success, project organization, recommended changes for similar projects, techniques used to overcome obstacles, strengths and weaknesses, team recommendations, projected vs. actual impact, team members.
7 Celebrate success Involve everyone who played a role; hold it away from the workplace; personally recognize outstanding performers. This is about the team, not the PM.
````` ::: ::: ### What prevents effective closeout - Getting the project **signed off** discourages the other closeout activities. - The **assumed urgency** of every project pressures the team to cut corners on the back end. - Closeout is given **low priority** and easily ignored. - **Lessons learned** is dismissed as a bookkeeping chore. - People assume that because every project is unique, **carryover is minimal**. - People just want to **move on** to the next challenge. ### Try it yourself: the seven elements in order ```{=html}
``` ## Project failure **Failure** = the project does not deliver what was required, judged against the **acceptance criteria** of the sponsor and customer, and can be triggered by changes in **scope, cost, or time**. **Early warning signs:** - Lack of viable **commercial objectives** - Lack of sufficient **decision-making authority** - **Market volatility** - **Low priority** assigned to the project **When to consider cancelling:** - Costs **exceed the business benefits** - The project no longer meets **strategic-fit** criteria - **Deadlines** keep being missed - **Technology evolves** beyond the project's scope ### Worked Example 1: continue or cancel? A project has already spent **\$480 000** (sunk). Finishing it needs another **\$260 000**. The product, if delivered, is now worth an estimated **\$300 000** in benefit --- the market moved while you were building. Live cell --- change the cost to finish or the remaining benefit. ```{=html}

Continue-or-Cancel Calculator

$
$
$
```
Show the live R code behind this calculator The card above re-runs this exact webR code every time you change an input, substituting your values for the variables at the top. Edit the code directly and press **Run Code** to experiment further. ```{webr-r} #| label: cancel-decision-13 sunk <- 480000 # already spent -- IRRELEVANT to the decision cost_to_finish <- 260000 remaining_benefit <- 300000 net_if_continue <- remaining_benefit - cost_to_finish money <- function(x) paste0(ifelse(x < 0, "-", ""), "$", format(round(abs(x)), big.mark = " ", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)) par(mar = c(5, 5, 3, 1), cex.main = 1.3, cex.lab = 1.2, cex.axis = 1.1) barplot(c("Sunk\n(ignore)" = sunk, "Cost to\nfinish" = cost_to_finish, "Remaining\nbenefit" = remaining_benefit) / 1000, col = c("#bdc3c7", "#e67e22", ifelse(net_if_continue > 0, "#16a085", "#e74c3c")), ylab = "$ thousand", main = "Only the last two bars matter") if (net_if_continue > 0) { cat("CONTINUE: the remaining benefit still beats the remaining cost\n") } else { cat(sprintf("!!CANCEL!!: finishing loses money from here, regardless of the %s already gone\n", money(sunk))) } cat(sprintf("Sunk cost (ignore it) %s\n", money(sunk))) cat(sprintf("Cost to finish %s\n", money(cost_to_finish))) cat(sprintf("Benefit if finished %s\n", money(remaining_benefit))) cat(sprintf("Net from *here* %s\n", money(net_if_continue))) ```
The \$480 000 is a **sunk cost** --- it is spent whether you continue or not, so it must not enter the decision. From here, spending \$260 000 to get \$300 000 is still worth \$40 000. (The sunk-cost fallacy --- "we've come too far to stop" --- is what keeps doomed projects alive.) ### Try it yourself: what counts in the decision? ```{=html}
``` ### Try it yourself: the cancel decision under uncertainty ```{=html}

Show the live R code behind this calculator The card above re-runs this exact webR code every time you change an input, substituting your values for the variables at the top. Edit the code directly and press **Run Code** to experiment further. ```{webr-r} #| label: cancel-decision-13b sunk <- 480000 cost_to_finish <- 260000 # The remaining benefit is uncertain -- try a range of market outcomes. benefit_weak <- 150000 benefit_below <- 250000 benefit_plan <- 300000 benefit_strong <- 400000 benefits <- c(benefit_weak, benefit_below, benefit_plan, benefit_strong) net <- benefits - cost_to_finish money <- function(x) paste0(ifelse(x < 0, "-", ""), "$", format(round(abs(x)), big.mark = " ", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)) smoney <- function(x) paste0(ifelse(x < 0, "-", "+"), "$", format(round(abs(x)), big.mark = " ", trim = TRUE)) par(mar = c(5, 5, 3, 1), cex.main = 1.3, cex.lab = 1.2, cex.axis = 1.1) barplot(net / 1000, names.arg = c("Weak", "Below plan", "On plan", "Strong"), col = ifelse(net > 0, "#16a085", "#e74c3c"), ylab = "Net from here ($ thousand)", main = "Net value of finishing, by outcome") abline(h = 0, lwd = 2) cat(sprintf("Break-even benefit: %s\n", money(cost_to_finish))) cat(sprintf("Sunk cost (ignored) %s\n", money(sunk))) for (i in seq_along(benefits)) { verdict <- if (net[i] > 0) "CONTINUE" else "!!CANCEL!!" cat(sprintf("If benefit = %s net %s: %s\n", money(benefits[i]), smoney(net[i]), verdict)) } ```
### Try it yourself: continue or cancel, with an uncertain benefit The sunk cost is given on purpose: it should not change your answers. Each team picks its own **data set**. ```{=html}
```
Show the worked solution The sunk cost never enters. Data set 1: expected benefit = 0.6 x \$260 000 + 0.4 x \$100 000 = \$196 000; less the \$180 000 still to spend, finishing is worth **+\$16 000** from here. The break-even benefit is simply the cost to finish, \$180 000. In data set 2 the expected benefit (\$116 000) falls short of the \$150 000 needed, so cancel, however much has been spent.
## Lessons from spectacular failures ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Cost overrun as a multiple of the original budget for three well-documented failures. Project Taurus (London Stock Exchange) ran to roughly 132 times its first budget before being abandoned after 11 years.](13-Project-Closeout-and-Termination_files/figure-html/fig-overruns-13-1.png){#fig-overruns-13 fig-align='center' width=912} ::: ::: - **Bank of America "MasterNet"** (1984) --- trust-department automation. Over budget by \$35M, rising toward \$80M; a 1988 failure meant loss of control over billions in trust accounts, all eventually recovered, but the **entire 255-person department was let go** as depositors fled. *Cause: scope and complexity understood far too late.* - **Future Imagery Architecture** (US spy satellites, 1997) --- bid won by a contractor that had never built an imaging satellite; internal estimate already predicted a \$4B overrun. **Testing was cut to save money**; a subcontractor's undisclosed manufacturing change caused gyroscope defects undiscovered for three years; costs reached ~\$18B by 2005. *Cause: unqualified bidder, cut testing, uncontrolled change.* - **Canadian Firearms Registry** (1995) --- estimated at \$119M to implement; a 2002 audit projected ~**\$1B**. *Causes: scope not understood, no plan for inter-agency cooperation, inconsistent data criteria, cost cover-up, no measurement of whether the registry actually worked.* - **Channel Tunnel** (budgeted 1979, opened 1994, one year late) --- final cost roughly **double** the original budget. - **Project Taurus** (London Stock Exchange paperless settlement, 1983) --- abandoned after **11 years** at ~**132 times** its original budget after switching to an incompatible US system that clashed with British finance law. **The recurring threads:** scope not truly understood; optimism and cost concealment; cutting testing to save money; no plan for the interfaces between organizations; and pressing on past every off-ramp because of sunk cost. ### Try it yourself: the final project reconciliation ```{=html}

Project Reconciliation Calculator

weeks
weeks
$

```
Show the live R code behind this calculator The card above re-runs this exact webR code every time you change an input, substituting your values for the variables at the top. Edit the code directly and press **Run Code** to experiment further. ```{webr-r} #| label: reconciliation-13 # Planned vs actual for the RC-vehicle prototype project at closeout. planned_weeks <- 30 actual_weeks <- 34 planned_cost <- 620000 actual_cost <- 703000 planned_scope_items <- 12 delivered_items <- 12 # all deliverables met sched_var_pct <- 100 * (actual_weeks - planned_weeks) / planned_weeks cost_var_pct <- 100 * (actual_cost - planned_cost) / planned_cost money <- function(x) paste0(ifelse(x < 0, "-", ""), "$", format(round(abs(x)), big.mark = " ", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)) par(mar = c(5, 5, 3, 1), cex.main = 1.3, cex.lab = 1.2, cex.axis = 1.1) bp <- barplot(c(Schedule = sched_var_pct, Cost = cost_var_pct), col = ifelse(c(sched_var_pct, cost_var_pct) < 20, "#2980b9", "#e74c3c"), ylim = c(min(0, sched_var_pct, cost_var_pct) * 1.2, max(25, sched_var_pct, cost_var_pct) * 1.15), ylab = "Variance vs. plan (%)", main = "Variance vs. the 20% threshold") abline(h = 0, lwd = 2) abline(h = 20, lty = 2, lwd = 2, col = "#e74c3c") success <- delivered_items == planned_scope_items && cost_var_pct < 20 && sched_var_pct < 20 if (success) { cat(sprintf("%s\n", if (sched_var_pct > 0 || cost_var_pct > 0) "SUCCESS with overruns" else "SUCCESS")) } else { cat("!!TROUBLED!!\n") } cat(sprintf("Schedule %g -> %g wk (%+.1f%%)\n", planned_weeks, actual_weeks, sched_var_pct)) cat(sprintf("Cost %s -> %s (%+.1f%%)\n", money(planned_cost), money(actual_cost), cost_var_pct)) cat(sprintf("Scope %g of %g deliverables accepted\n", delivered_items, planned_scope_items)) cat(sprintf("Next step %s\n", if (success) "document the causes in the history file and lessons learned" else "the lessons-learned review is the priority deliverable")) ```
## Closing out the RC-vehicle project - **Verify scope** against the signed scope statement: all body options delivered, drop and EMC tests passed, compliance approvals in hand, retailer satisfaction confirmed. - **Closeout contracts**: settle final invoices with MCS/Paragon and the carbon-fibre supplier; return the customer's proprietary artwork. - **Administration**: return the borrowed design engineers and millwrights to their functional managers with completed performance reviews. - **Lessons learned**: the new-line learning curve and the unproven-supplier risk are the two entries that matter most for the next program. - **Termination by integration**: there is no separate support team; the prototype team is **reabsorbed into production engineering** for the 100 000-unit run. - **Celebrate** --- away from the plant, with everyone who contributed. ## Key Takeaways - Termination provides **sponsor acceptance, complete records, as-built documentation, and retained lessons learned.** - Types: **extinction** (stopped), **addition** (becomes permanent), **integration** (reabsorbed), **starvation** (slow deliberate neglect). - Work the **seven elements**: verify scope, close contracts, close administration, lessons learned, history file, final report, celebrate. - Closeout fails because sign-off feels like "done", the next project is louder, and lessons learned is treated as bookkeeping. Resist all three. - **Cancel** when the **cost to complete exceeds the remaining benefit** --- the money already spent is **sunk** and irrelevant to that decision. - Famous failures share the same causes: **scope not understood, cost concealed, testing cut, interfaces unplanned, sunk-cost momentum.** ## Case Study: Meridian R/C — Week 13 ::: {.callout-tip .case-study title="📁 CASE STUDY FILE — Week 13: The Trailblazer Ships"} Thirteen weeks after Daniel Cho signed a $800,000 charter for a single prototype, you close the file on the Meridian Trailblazer with a phone call from Renata Ford. The drop/durability test (activity G) and the toy-safety certification (activity H) — the two milestones every other decision this quarter was built to protect — both pass. Kestrel Retail Group approves the prototype and awards Meridian the **100,000-unit production contract** for next year's holiday season. The bet you made in Week 1, choosing aluminium over steel and carbon fibre for the body and frame, paid off exactly as planned: durable enough to pass, affordable enough to scale. This is a **termination by integration**, not addition: there is no separate production-support team to hand the project to, because the project *becomes* production. Priya Nandakumar and Sofia Reyes are reassigned directly into production engineering, carrying the tooling and testing knowledge they built over thirteen weeks straight into the ramp-up. Marcus Webb stays on supplier contracts, now renegotiating MCS's $136,000 motor-and-controller price at 100,000-unit volume instead of prototype volume. You report to Daniel Cho a final Estimate at Completion of **~$798,000** against his $800,000 ceiling — effectively on budget, a margin of about $2,100 that vindicates the bottom-up number Daniel questioned so hard back in Week 9. Closing the history file, three lessons learned carry forward into the production program. First, the **$9,000 MCS negotiation saving** from Week 10: using the Paragon quote as leverage, without ever intending to switch suppliers, protected both the proven vendor relationship and the schedule. Second, **Priya's Week 11 overallocation**, resolved by shifting frame tooling (activity D) inside its own ten days of float rather than adding headcount — proof that a resource conflict is not always a hiring problem. Third, the **Week 2 communication near-miss**, where a spec change missed Kestrel's Vancouver buyer and cost three days and $4,000 — the RACI matrix adopted afterward is the reason the Week 13 sign-off reached every stakeholder the first time. The schedule, the budget, the people, and the lessons all land in the same file: the Trailblazer prototype is finished, and the production program it built starts from everything this one got right. ::: ## Practice Problems
Problem 1: Sunk cost trap A project has consumed \$1.2M of a \$1.5M budget. Finishing needs \$500 000 (the last \$300 000 of budget plus a \$200 000 overrun). The delivered product is now worth \$350 000. The sponsor says "we've spent \$1.2M --- we can't stop now." Evaluate.
Solution ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cost_to_finish <- 500000 remaining_benefit <- 350000 cat(sprintf("Net from here: $%s - $%s = $%s\n", format(remaining_benefit, big.mark = " "), format(cost_to_finish, big.mark = " "), format(remaining_benefit - cost_to_finish, big.mark = " "))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Net from here: $350 000 - $5e+05 = $-150 000 ``` ::: ::: Finishing turns \$500 000 of new spend into \$350 000 of value --- a \$150 000 loss **from today**. The \$1.2M is gone either way. Cancel (or de-scope until the remaining cost drops below \$350 000). "We can't stop now" is the sunk-cost fallacy.
Problem 2: Which termination type? 1. An automaker keeps its vehicle-launch team on as the permanent production-support team. 2. A cancelled R&D project's engineers return to the design department. 3. A failed pilot is shut down, its budget audited, its test rig sold. 4. A VP's favourite project keeps a \$1/year budget so it stays "active" on paper.
Answers 1. **Addition.** 2. **Integration.** 3. **Extinction.** 4. **Starvation.**
Problem 3 (discussion): the team wants to skip lessons learned The RC-vehicle project delivered late and over budget but the product passed. The exhausted team wants to skip the lessons-learned review and start on the production ramp. As PM, what do you do and why?
Discussion points This is exactly the moment the review matters most --- a troubled project is where the carryover value is highest, and the next program will hit the *same* new-line learning curve and *same* supplier risk. Keep it short and structured, focus on **what went wrong and why** (not blame), capture 2--3 concrete, assigned actions, and put it in the history file before the team disperses and the memory fades. Skipping it guarantees the next project repeats the overrun.
